taxonomic_note: Legacy Master Plant Pool name Tridens eragrostoides normalized to current accepted Triplasiella eragrostoides.
look_here_first: LOVEGRASS TRIDENS (Triplasiella eragrostoides; old Tridens/Triodia names): two REAL source-labelled mature open-panicle pictures help recognition, but purpletop, Texas tridens and purple lovegrass also have spreading heads. In the SECOND photo, the stiff bristly RIGHT-BACKGROUND grass is NOT this species. Confirm one mature true 3-veined lemma (~2–3 mm) with ONLY midnerve prolonged as a short mucro (not three long awns) plus inner membranous lacerate 1–3-mm ligule, and actual rooted plant. Research clue: Hagenbuch & Lemke 2015 list a Hays County Tharp s.n. TEX-LL voucher under Tridens eragrostoides; ORIGINAL specimen has not been inspected, county hold remains PROVISIONAL.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays-local source; Kew accepts Triplasiella eragrostoides and explicitly lists Tridens eragrostoides as a synonym.

morphology_keys.family_pattern: Poaceae: use growth habit, ligule, panicle architecture, spikelet form, lemma hairs and awns. For this old Tridens complex, panicle openness/color and current genus placement are especially useful.
best_field_traits: Open, spreading fine-branched panicle with small scattered spikelets. Purpletop/Texas tridens/lovegrasses ALSO have open heads, so this is a first clue only.

Tufted perennial; ACTUAL rooted base is not pictured. Texas Hill Country field treatment (2015) reports rhizomes and stolons ABSENT for Tridens eragrostoides, whereas the broader Flora Neomexicana Triplasiella generic diagnosis describes knotty rhizomatous bases. Distinguish true horizontal node-bearing rhizomes from a merely hard knotty crown on one documented living specimen; do not assert either with certainty from current head-only photographs.

Mature 3-veined lemma roughly 2–3.5 mm; central midnerve may extend as SHORT point/mucro, lateral veins do NOT form three equally projecting prongs in regional key. No current photograph resolves the veins.

ACTUAL true INNER blade/sheath is a 1–3 mm membranous ligule with a lacerate margin according to the Texas Hill Country vegetative treatment for Tridens eragrostoides. Generic Flora Neomexicana also discusses a ciliate membrane; do not conflate lacerate edges with a hair-only ligule or claim either appearance has been photographed for this source individual.

Open panicle with arching to spreading/drooping branches, broadly 10–30 cm long by 8–20 cm wide in taxonomic treatment; these values are reference context, NOT a size measured in current source photos.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: The airy lovegrass-like seedhead is the main cue. It is much more open than white tridens and now belongs in Triplasiella.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: FIRST: one physically archived CC BY/CC0/CC BY-SA photo of T. eragrostoides measured mature 3-veined lemma with central point and glumes, showing true size and all floret boundaries.
SECOND: true 1–3 mm ragged MEMBRANOUS ligule revealed at actual blade/sheath inner surface with a 1-mm ruler and precise arrow.

THIRD: a source-identified intact flowering plant with its actual fibrous-root crown exposed and centimeter ruler; check for a knotty crown and independently demonstrate whether horizontal, node-bearing rhizomes or stolons are REALLY PRESENT. Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015) report absence in Texas Hill Country material; Flora Neomexicana generic treatment describes knotty rhizomatous bases. Do not infer presence without same-voucher structural evidence.
FOURTH: matched macro comparison with native Tridens flavus and T. texanus mature lemma apex, not just whole flowerheads.
FIFTH: verify original photo-2 species voucher/GBIF photo-level license and ensure unrelated background grass is not mistaken for target.
crew_field_check: 1. Distinguish the foreground Triplasiella in photos 1–2 from unrelated BRISTLY grass at upper right in photo 2.
2. Compare photos 3–5: purpletop, Texas tridens and purple lovegrass are other native species with overlapping airy flowering heads. NEVER decide from one flowerhead silhouette.
3. Confirm a mature target spikelet and short 3-veined lemma under 10–20x beside a 1-mm ruler, glumes visible. No actual macro in current gallery.
4. Open actual blade/sheath and measure ragged membranous ligule. No actual macro in current gallery.
5. Preserve T. eragrostoides existing provisional Hays occurrence. This is not a finished county provenance audit.

comparisons.key_distinctions: TARGET Triplasiella eragrostoides — fairly broad open panicle, fine distant branches, darkening small spikelets; prior name Tridens eragrostoides. A midnerve that alone extends as a short projection is a useful fine distinction in Flora Neomexicana. NATIVE purpletop Tridens flavus — spreading/drooping OPEN panicle too, often purplish; beware previous overgeneralization that all Tridens are contracted. NATIVE Texas tridens Tridens texanus — arching open panicle, potentially quite similar from several feet away. Measure/inspect mature spikelet and lemma instead of using panicle outline as sole key. NATIVE purple lovegrass Eragrostis spectabilis — airy colored panicle and tuft, often superficially similar; check florets/lemma architecture in a confirmed plant. Triplasiella vs sandgrass Triplasis: the 2016 taxonomic treatment reports MUCH broader target panicles and different palea keels, plus absence of upper-sheath cleistogamous spikelets; those features are not verified in current images.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · OPEN HEAD
field_id_short_tiles.short: Broad loose branching is a clue, not an ID
field_id_short_tiles.details: Actual locally archived species photographs (panels 0 and 1) show very open thin panicles and small separated reddish spikelets; panel 1 contains a completely DIFFERENT unlabelled bristly seedhead in its top-right background. A NEW arrow explicitly warns the crew not to transfer those bristles to Triplasiella. Neither the photos nor the person's hand provide exact spikelet size, true ligule, root or 3-veined lemma proof. Hays County Tharp s.n. TEX-LL is cited in the 2015 Texas Hill Country herbarium appendix but underlying voucher not reexamined.
field_id_short_tiles.status: TWO REAL OPEN PANICLES + NEGATIVE BACKGROUND-PLANT ARROW; EXACT ANATOMY PENDING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · CHECK NATIVES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Purpletop and Texas tridens are also open!
field_id_short_tiles.details: Native LOOK-ALIKE photos in panels 2, 3, 4 respectively belong to purpletop (Tridens flavus), Texas tridens (Tridens texanus) and purple lovegrass (Eragrostis spectabilis). Purpletop can have an airy broadly spreading/drooping panicle TOO. Their glumes and mature lemma sizes must be examined as independent different-species specimens. Do not treat any image of them as a photograph of Triplasiella's true lemma or collar.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MICROSCOPE LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Real 3-veined 2–3 mm lemma + midnerve point still unphotographed
field_id_short_tiles.details: Flora Neomexicana's diagnostic key gives the target mature lemma approx. 2–3 mm with ONLY the MIDNERVE extending beyond the tip as a tiny point; purpletop generally larger with multiple nerve tips protruding. A vouchered detached 3-veined lemma dorsal-face-up beside a REAL 1-mm ruler at 10–20× is required; current source photos 0/1 show spikelets too distant to count veins, and the 1900 exact-taxon Fig. 97(d) is a PRINTED BOTANICAL DRAWING, NOT a photographed scale macro. Preserve scientific hold pending such an original photo.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · TRUE COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: True 1–3 mm lacerate membrane; verify source-specific margin
field_id_short_tiles.details: The published 2015 Texas Hill Country treatment describes a 1–3-mm membranous LIGULE, obtuse to acute with distinctly LACERATE margin at actual INNER blade/sheath junction, along with a continuous glabrous collar, absent auricles and OPEN leaf sheath. This is stronger local vegetative key evidence than guessing a membrane from generic Tridens photos. A competing broader regional generic treatment describes a CILIATE membrane. The current gallery photographs no original open INNER ligule. Obtain 1-mm ruler showing its free margin, back of membrane and actual leaf attachment to the same voucher.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · ROOTED PERENNIAL
field_id_short_tiles.short: Actual perennial tuft crown missing; published rhizome accounts disagree
field_id_short_tiles.details: Hagenbuch and Lemke's 2015 Texas Hill Country vegetative key specifically describes Tridens eragrostoides as perennial and cespitose, with RHIZOMES AND STOLONS ABSENT; shoots originate from actual basal crown. Flora Neomexicana's later general genus treatment instead describes tufted plants with knotty RHIZOMATOUS bases. Those descriptions may reflect interpretation/scope, not proof of an individual rhizome. No present photograph shows the rootstock at all. Document one flowering plant continuously from crown into mature panicle, with root tips, actual lateral underground stems (IF PRESENT), nodes/buds and a centimeter ruler; NEVER claim a hidden rhizome.
field_id_short_tiles.status: SOURCE CONFLICT HELD — NEEDS SAME-VOUCHER ROOT PHOTOGRAPH

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · MATURE FLORET SPLIT
field_id_short_tiles.short: One tiny midnerve point—not three long awns
field_id_short_tiles.details: Three-way crew decision: photograph ONE source-verified mature target floret (lower+upper glumes, lemma, palea) with exact 1-mm ruler; check 3 lemma veins and whether ONLY central midnerve projects as a short mucro. Do not call the point a long awn. Compare an isolated mature purpletop lemma (larger, more projecting nerve ends) at SAME scale. Re-photograph inner 1–3-mm lacerate membranous ligule plus actual rooted crown on specimen, because the Texas Hill Country key vs broader Flora Neomexicana disagree on rhizomes and ligule fringe; the gallery does not settle them.
